An addendum is a piece of extra information that is added to a document, book, contract, email, or any piece of writing — after that writing has already been completed or finalized.

Think of it this way: you write something, you finish it, you consider it done — and then you realize there's something extra that needs to be included. So you attach that extra piece at the end. That extra piece is the addendum.

The word itself is used to label or refer to that addition.

Three things define an addendum:

  1. It comes after. The original document was already finished before the addendum was created. The addendum is not part of the original — it's a late addition.
  2. It adds, not corrects. An addendum brings in new information that was missing or wasn't available earlier. It doesn't fix a mistake in the original (that's a different thing — see below).
  3. It belongs with the original. An addendum is attached to or presented alongside the original document. It's not a standalone piece — it only makes sense in the context of the original.

The word "addendum" appears most often in formal or professional settings:

  • Contracts and legal documents — A contract is signed, but both parties agree to add a new clause or condition. That new clause is attached as an addendum. Neither party has to rewrite the entire contract; the addendum simply tags along with it.
  • Books and academic papers — An author finishes a book, but by the time it's published, new research has come out. The author adds a short section at the end to address this. That section is an addendum.
  • Reports and business documents — A company report is submitted, and then additional data arrives. The extra data sheet attached to the report is an addendum.
  • Emails and letters — Less formally, someone might write an email, send it, and then quickly write a follow-up saying "One more thing I forgot to mention..." — that follow-up is, in spirit, an addendum (even if they don't use the word).

The plural of addendum is addenda (the traditional form) or addendums (the modern English form). Both are correct and widely accepted.

  • "The contract had two addenda attached to it."
  • "She sent the report with three addendums."

In formal writing — especially legal, academic, or medical writing — addenda is more common. In everyday professional writing, addendums is perfectly fine.
How it differs from similar words

Several words are close to "addendum" in meaning, but they're not the same:

  • Appendix — Also a section added at the end of a document, but an appendix is usually planned from the start as part of the document (like statistical tables at the back of a research paper). An addendum, by contrast, is something that wasn't planned — it's added afterward because something was overlooked or changed.
  • Amendment — An amendment changes or modifies what was already written. An addendum only adds without touching the original. So if a contract clause is reworded, that's an amendment. If a brand-new clause is added, that's an addendum.
  • Erratum / Errata — These refer to corrections of errors in a published work. If a book says "the population was 4 million" but it should be "40 million," the correction notice is errata. An addendum isn't about fixing errors — it's about adding information.
  • Supplement — A supplement can mean something added to make a whole thing more complete, but it often implies a larger, more substantial addition — sometimes even a separate publication. An addendum tends to be shorter and directly tied to one specific document.
  • Postscript (P.S.) — A postscript is the informal note you add at the end of a letter after your signature ("P.S. Don't forget to call me!"). An addendum is more formal, more substantial, and more likely to carry real weight in a document.

• "Before signing, please read the addendum at the end of the agreement — it outlines the new warranty terms."
  • "The professor distributed an addendum to the syllabus after the course dates changed."
  • "The final report included an addendum with data that wasn't available when the report was first written."
  • "An addendum to the original study was published the following year, incorporating feedback from peer reviewers."
  • "The seller agreed to the buyer's request and attached an addendum to the purchase agreement."
When you would use this word yourself

You'd use "addendum" (or "addenda"/"addendums") when:

  • You need to refer to something that was added to a finished document.
  • You want to label an extra piece of writing you're attaching to something you've already submitted or sent.
  • You're telling someone to look at additional material that accompanies a document.

For example, if you send a report and later realize you forgot to include a section, you might write: "Please find attached an addendum to the report I sent yesterday."
An addendum is an addition made to a completed document — something tacked on at the end because it was missed, forgotten, or newly available, without changing anything that was already there.
